newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Canada's U.S. ambassador to go to Zaire for U.N.
newsitem.headline: Canada's U.S. ambassador to go to Zaire for U.N.

text.p: The United Nations is set to appoint Canada's ambassador to Washington as its new representative to deal with warfare and the refugee crisis in eastern Zaire, U.N. sources said on Tuesday.

But the envoy, Raymond A.J. Chretien, nephew of Canada's prime minister, Jean Chretien, will only serve for a month as an interim representative until a more permanent mission can be established. He leaves for the region on November 6, reportedly on a nine-seater jet supplied by Canada.
Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali last Friday called for an emergency mission to go to Zaire followed by an international conference to prevent warfare spreading throughout central Africa.

But before a conference could be convened, he said a "provisional solution" had to be found to end the fighting in eastern Zaire. He said he wanted to send a team with a new mediator to begin negotiations leading to a conference.

Highly regarded in Washington, Chretien's most recent efforts involved persuading President Bill Clinton to delay U.S. sanctions against Canada over trade with Cuba. He is one of the few francophones to be appointed to Washington, a position traditionally reserved for anglophones.
Diplomats said they expected a letter to the Security Council from Boutros-Ghali shortly on the appointment, which has been approved informally by the key council members.

Fighting is raging in eastern Zaire between Rwandan Tutsis, who have lived in the region since the 18th century, and the Zairean army, which says Tutsi soldiers from Rwanda and Burundi have joined the conflict.

The eastern Zaire region also is host to Hutus who fled Rwanda fearing revenge attacks after the 1994 massacre of up to a million minority Tutsis and moderate Hutus. Nearly 600,000 Hutus in Zaire are on the move to avoid the fighting, with relief officials unable to reach most of them.
